title: Advance care planning, ReSPECT and DNACPR
blurb: Tell apart advance statements, ADRTs, LPAs, ReSPECT plans and DNACPR decisions, and know which ones bind you.
question: Mrs Kowalczyk, 79, has a ReSPECT form recommending ward-based care without CPR. She also wrote a signed, witnessed advance decision refusing artificial ventilation 'even if my life is at risk'. She now lacks capacity and is deteriorating. Which document legally binds the team, and which guides them?

teach.h: Planning ahead for a time you cannot speak
teach.body: Advance care planning is a voluntary conversation about what matters to a person and how they want to be cared for if they lose capacity. It can produce several different records, and the nurse must know their legal weight. Some bind clinicians (a valid and applicable advance decision to refuse treatment; a decision by a registered attorney within their authority). Others guide decisions (advance statements, ReSPECT recommendations).

teach.caption: MCA s4(6)(a): best interests must consider the person's past wishes, in particular any relevant written statement made when they had capacity.

head: Requirement
Detail
rows: Both the decision and the statement
By P, or by another in P's presence at P's direction
P signs or acknowledges before a witness, who signs in P's presence
Applies 'even if life is at risk'
teach.caption: Withdrawal needs capacity but need not be in writing. An ADRT is not valid if a later LPA gives the attorney authority over the same treatment (s25(2)(b)).

teach.h: Is this ADRT valid and applicable?

children.edge: Withdrawn, or later LPA covers it
children.label: Not valid

teach.caption: MCA s25(2)–(4). Life-sustaining refusals must also meet the s25(5)–(6) formalities.

teach.body: A lasting power of attorney is not created unless it is registered with the Office of the Public Guardian (s9(2)(b)). A health and welfare attorney acts only when the person lacks capacity for the decision (s11(7)), and can refuse life-sustaining treatment only if the LPA expressly says so (s11(8)). Always check the registered document and its scope before relying on an attorney's decision.

ReSPECT creates personalised recommendations for a future emergency in which a person cannot make or express choices, through conversations with the person, family and professionals. The form is not legally binding: the clinicians present make the final decision unless a legally binding document such as an ADRT applies. A DNACPR decision applies only to CPR; all other appropriate treatment and care continues.
teach.cite: RCUK ReSPECT page; RCUK Ethics 2025; BMA/RCUK/RCN Decisions relating to CPR (3rd ed.) s5.1

teach.caption: Tracey [2014] EWCA Civ 822: Article 8 is engaged; there should be a presumption in favour of consulting the patient unless it would cause physical or psychological harm.

teach.h: Scenario: Mrs Kowalczyk on the respiratory ward
teach.body: Staff nurse Ben reads both documents. The ADRT refusing ventilation is in writing, signed, witnessed and says it applies even if her life is at risk, and nothing suggests she withdrew it or made a later LPA. It is valid and applicable, so ventilation must not be given. The ReSPECT form guides the team towards ward-based treatment such as antibiotics and oxygen; the doctors present weigh it in her best interests. Her DNACPR decision means no CPR, not no care.

teach.text: Don't treat a ReSPECT form or a DNACPR as a refusal of all treatment. DNACPR covers CPR alone; ReSPECT gives non-binding recommendations. The legally binding refusal is a valid, applicable ADRT. And don't treat an advance statement as binding: it is weighed in best interests.

items: Advance statement: wishes and values, not binding, must be considered in best interests.
ADRT: 18+, with capacity, refusals only; binding if valid and applicable; life-sustaining needs writing, signature, witness and 'even if life is at risk'.
LPA must be registered; attorney acts only when capacity is lost; life-sustaining refusals need express authority.
ReSPECT: recommendations for emergencies, not legally binding.
DNACPR applies only to CPR; consult the patient unless there is a convincing reason not to (Tracey).
Preferred place of care and death is part of planning; explain when wishes cannot be met (NICE NG31).

summary: You can now explain the legal weight of advance statements, ADRTs, LPAs, ReSPECT plans and DNACPR decisions. You can also check an ADRT for validity and applicability and apply the duty to consult before a DNACPR decision.

A.q: Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, who can make an advance decision to refuse treatment?
options: A person aged 16 or over with capacity
A person aged 18 or over with capacity
A registered health and welfare attorney
The person's GP after a best interests meeting
A.why: MCA s24(1): an advance decision is made by a person who has reached 18 and has capacity to make it.

whyNot.0: Sixteen is the age from which most of the MCA applies, but ADRTs require the person to be 18.
whyNot.2: An attorney makes decisions on the person's behalf; an ADRT is the person's own advance refusal.
whyNot.3: A clinician cannot make an advance decision for someone; it must be the person's own.

A.q: Hamza, 70, has a DNACPR decision. Overnight he develops a fever and becomes breathless with a new productive cough. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Withhold antibiotics, as he is for comfort care
Escalate and treat the infection as usual
Contact his family before any treatment
Move him to a side room for end of life care
A.why: A DNACPR decision applies only to CPR (BMA/RCUK/RCN guidance s5.1). All other appropriate treatment, including antibiotics and escalation, continues unless separately decided.

whyNot.0: DNACPR does not mean comfort care alone; treatment decisions are separate.
whyNot.2: Families may be informed, but urgent treatment should not wait for them when it is clinically indicated.
whyNot.3: Nothing suggests he is dying; a DNACPR alone does not mean end of life care.

A.q: Which statement about a ReSPECT form is accurate?
options: It is legally binding on paramedics and doctors
It replaces the need for a capacity assessment
It records recommendations that are not legally binding
It can be made by family when the person lacks capacity
A.why: RCUK: ReSPECT preferences and recommendations are recorded on a non-legally binding form; the final decision rests with the clinicians present unless a legally binding document applies.

whyNot.0: ReSPECT recommendations guide clinicians but do not bind them in law.
whyNot.1: Capacity still has to be assessed for each decision at the time.
whyNot.3: Families take part in the conversations, but the plan records clinical recommendations agreed through the process, not a family decision.

B.q: Bridie, 74, made a written ADRT refusing artificial ventilation, but it does not state that it applies even if her life is at risk. She now lacks capacity and needs ventilation to survive. What is the legal position?
options: The ADRT is binding because it is in writing
The ADRT is binding if her family confirm her wishes
The ADRT is not applicable to life-sustaining treatment
The ADRT is binding but must first be confirmed by a court
B.why: MCA s25(5): an ADRT is not applicable to life-sustaining treatment unless it is verified by a statement that it applies even if life is at risk, and meets the writing, signature and witness requirements.

whyNot.0: Being in writing is necessary but not sufficient; the 'even if life is at risk' statement is also required.
whyNot.1: Family confirmation cannot cure a missing statutory formality.
whyNot.3: No court confirmation is needed for a valid ADRT; this one fails the formalities.

B.q: In 2020 Frank made a valid ADRT refusing tube feeding. In 2024, with capacity, he created and registered a health and welfare LPA giving his son authority over tube feeding. Frank now lacks capacity. Whose decision governs tube feeding?
options: The 2020 ADRT
His son as attorney
The consultant alone
The Court of Protection
B.why: MCA s25(2)(b): an ADRT is not valid if the person later creates an LPA giving the attorney authority over the same treatment. The son, as registered attorney, decides in Frank's best interests.

whyNot.0: The later LPA covering the same treatment makes the earlier ADRT invalid.
whyNot.2: The consultant advises, but the attorney holds the authority for this decision.
whyNot.3: The court is a last resort for disputes; the attorney has authority here.

B.q: A registrar plans to complete a DNACPR form for Lionel, 71, who has capacity, without telling him, because 'it will only upset him'. What should the nurse advocate?
options: That the family are told instead of Lionel
That the form is completed and discussed at discharge
That a second doctor countersigns so no discussion is needed
That Lionel is consulted unless it would cause him harm
B.why: Tracey [2014]: there is a presumption in favour of consulting the patient about a DNACPR decision unless there is a convincing reason not to, such as a risk of physical or psychological harm. Lord Dyson MR warned against being too ready to exclude patients because involvement may distress them; distress alone is unlikely to be enough unless it is likely to cause harm.

whyNot.0: Lionel has capacity, so the discussion is with him, not instead of him.
whyNot.1: Delaying the discussion until discharge means he is not consulted at the time of the decision.
whyNot.2: A second signature does not replace the duty to consult the patient.

C.q: Pearl, 86, has advanced dementia. Years ago, with capacity, she wrote a signed note saying she would 'like to stay at home with my cats until the end'. She now lacks capacity and a care home move is proposed. How should the note be used?
options: As a binding refusal of a care home placement
As irrelevant because she now lacks capacity
As her wishes to weigh in a best interests decision
As consent to remain at home whatever the level of risk
C.why: This is an advance statement of wishes. Under MCA s4(6)(a) best interests must consider past wishes, in particular any relevant written statement made with capacity, but it is not legally binding.

whyNot.0: An advance statement is not a binding refusal; ADRTs cover refusal of treatment, not accommodation.
whyNot.1: Her past wishes remain highly relevant to best interests.
whyNot.3: It expresses a wish to be weighed; it does not operate as consent overriding risk.

C.q: Gerald, 88, lacks capacity and has pneumonia. His daughter shows a health and welfare LPA she says covers 'everything', but it has not been registered. She refuses antibiotics for him. What should the nurse do?
options: Follow her refusal, as she is acting as his attorney
Escalate: the unregistered LPA confers no authority
Ask her to sign a refusal form for the notes
Withhold antibiotics until the LPA is registered
C.why: MCA s9(2)(b): an LPA is not created unless it is registered with the Office of the Public Guardian. The team decide in Gerald's best interests, consulting his daughter.

whyNot.0: An unregistered LPA gives her no legal authority to refuse treatment.
whyNot.2: A signed form does not create authority she does not have.
whyNot.3: Registration can take time; withholding treatment meanwhile may harm him and is not lawful on this basis.

C.q: Elspeth, 80, has a ReSPECT form recommending no ICU admission. She has capacity and, during an acute illness, tells the doctor she now wants to be considered for intensive care. What should happen?
options: Treat her current, capacitous wishes as central
Follow the ReSPECT form, as it was agreed earlier
Ask her family to decide which wish applies
Seek a court ruling before any change
C.why: ReSPECT is for situations where the person cannot make or express choices and is not legally binding. With capacity, Elspeth takes part in decisions now, and the plan should be reviewed as circumstances change.

whyNot.1: A non-binding plan made earlier does not override the current wishes of a person with capacity.
whyNot.2: She has capacity, so the family cannot choose for her.
whyNot.3: A court is not needed; the plan is reviewed with her.

reteach.title: Binding or guiding?
reteach.question: Sort each document: does it bind the team, or guide them?

blocks.body: BINDING: a valid and applicable ADRT; a decision by a registered health and welfare attorney acting within their authority. GUIDING: advance statements of wishes, ReSPECT recommendations, preferred place of care. A DNACPR decision is a clinical decision about CPR only; it does not stop other treatment.

blocks.text: Any advance document stops applying while the person has capacity to decide now. Always ask the person first.

explain.body: Made at 18+ with capacity. Refusals only. For life-sustaining treatment: in writing, signed by P (or by another at P's direction in P's presence), witnessed, with a statement that it applies even if life is at risk. Can be withdrawn with capacity, verbally if wished.

letters.word: Statement: even if life at risk

test.q: Abdul, with capacity, tells his nurse he no longer wants his written ADRT refusing dialysis to apply. Must he withdraw it in writing?
options: Yes, signed and witnessed like the original
Yes, on the Office of the Public Guardian form
Yes, countersigned by his GP
No, he can withdraw it verbally
test.why: MCA s24(3)–(4): a person with capacity may withdraw an advance decision at any time, and the withdrawal need not be in writing. Record the withdrawal clearly.

whyNot.0: The formalities apply to making a life-sustaining ADRT, not to withdrawing one.
whyNot.1: The OPG registers LPAs; ADRTs are not registered with it.
whyNot.2: No professional countersignature is needed to withdraw.

explain.body: Not created unless registered with the Office of the Public Guardian. Acts only when the person lacks capacity for the decision. Refusing life-sustaining treatment needs express provision in the LPA.

test.q: A registered health and welfare attorney wants to refuse a life-sustaining treatment for her father. What must the LPA contain for this refusal to be valid?
options: A GP's signature on every page of the document
A copy of a recent mental capacity assessment
Express power over life-sustaining treatment
A supporting statement from two family witnesses
test.why: MCA s11(8): an attorney can refuse life-sustaining treatment only if the LPA contains express provision to that effect.

whyNot.0: No GP signature is required on the instrument.
whyNot.1: Capacity is assessed at the time of the decision; it is not part of the LPA document.
whyNot.3: No family witness statement is required for this power.

explain.body: Personalised recommendations for a future emergency where the person cannot make or express choices. Made through conversation. Not legally binding; clinicians present decide, unless a legally binding document applies. Reviewed if circumstances change.

items: Includes CPR within wider goals of care

test.q: A paramedic finds a ReSPECT form recommending hospital admission for treatment but no CPR. The person lacks capacity and is acutely unwell. Who makes the final treatment decision?
options: The clinicians present at the time
The GP who originally signed the form
The person's next of kin or carer
Resuscitation Council UK
test.why: RCUK: the final decision rests with the healthcare professionals responsible for the person's immediate care at that time, unless a legally binding document applies.

whyNot.1: The signing clinician's recommendation guides, but the clinicians present decide.
whyNot.2: Next of kin have no automatic decision-making authority for an adult.
whyNot.3: RCUK publishes guidance; it does not make individual decisions.

explain.body: Applies only to CPR. No obligation to offer CPR that would not succeed, but the patient should be informed and consulted unless there is a convincing reason not to (Tracey). Offer a second opinion if the decision is not accepted. Record and review.

test.q: Lionel's DNACPR has been discussed with him. He disagrees with it. What should be offered?
options: A second opinion
A referral to the coroner
Removal of the form from his notes
An IMCA referral
test.why: BMA/RCUK/RCN Decisions relating to CPR: if the decision is not accepted, a second opinion should be offered.

whyNot.1: The coroner investigates certain deaths, not treatment disagreements.
whyNot.2: Removing the record does not resolve the clinical disagreement.
whyNot.3: An IMCA is for people who lack capacity and have no one to consult; Lionel has capacity.
